Triple Black Corvette Restored to NCRS Standards, the Selling Price Is Obvious
27 photos
Photo: eBay seller capefear96terry
You won’t see many like this. A 1966 Chevrolet Corvette that has already been restored checks all the right boxes to impress the NCRS judges is trying to sell at a price that can hardly surprise anyone.
While the 1966 model year might not be as desirable as its predecessors - certainly not as desirable as the 1963 split-window coupe - this car is a rare triple-black configuration. It wears a beautiful black finish paired with a black cabin and a black top. It does look exquisite, and the restoration that was finished not long ago certainly made everything more eye-catching.
The car landed on eBay because it’s trying to find a new home. It’s now parked in the heated garage that’s been serving as shelter since the restoration was finished, and this is probably where it’ll continue to sleep until it leaves for a new garage.
Photo: eBay seller capefear96terry While the changes that took place in the engine lineup are probably the most notable on the 1966 Corvette, the thing I’ll always remember about this model year was the design of the backup lights. Chevrolet redesigned them and integrated them directly into the taillights for a reason that made perfect sense: backup lights were now standard on all Corvettes, so offering them outside the taillights no longer made sense.
Otherwise, yes, the engine lineup received one notable upgrade: a big-block - an actual big block - was now available. After going for a 396 in 1965, Chevrolet now launched a 427 that joined the lineup with two power configurations.
A 327 continued to be standard with 300 horsepower, while the L79 was the upgraded version of this engine with 350 horsepower. The L36 was the first big-block setup in the lineup, using a displacement of 427 cubic inches to produce 390 horsepower.
The L72 was the top configuration and was an upgraded version of the L36. It used a higher compression ratio - 11.0:1 versus 10.25:1 - and mechanical valve lifters versus hydraulic to produce 425 horsepower.
Photo: eBay seller capefear96terry The L72 wasn’t the rarest engine on the 1966 Corvette, despite being the most expensive at $312. This unit made its way to 5,528 Vettes, but fewer buyers - 5,116 - decided to pay less - $181.20 - for the upgrade to the 390-horsepower version.
Chevrolet ended the year with 27,720 Corvettes rolling off the assembly line, and the convertible was the more popular configuration with 17,762 units. The coupe accounted for 9,958 orders.
While this is a convertible, the triple black setup makes it significantly rarer. While I couldn’t find any production numbers - Chevrolet didn’t offer a breakdown by interior and top color - the documentation that sells with the car confirms this Corvette hasn’t been altered. It did leave the factory with this triple-black setup, and that’s precisely how it was restored and maintained.
The original build sheet indicates that the first buyer ordered the car in Tuxedo Black paired with the black trim and a black convertible top. He also paid extra for the side dual exhaust system, the PB AM/FM radio, and the 4-speed transmission.
The car was and still is powered by the 425-horsepower TurboJet engine. The engine received a complete refresh during the restoration, so everything is now in perfect shape. The car starts, runs, and drives beautifully, though it didn’t spend much time on the road after the restoration was finalized.
The car is “all matching numbers, including glass, carburetor, transmission, and rear,” the seller explains.
Photo: eBay seller capefear96terry At first glance, this Corvette has it all, and it’s hard to find a better convertible if you’re into this triple-black setup. Already restored and sporting the top engine you could get in 1966, this specimen will probably find a home eventually, though there’s no doubt this won’t happen overnight.
The reason is as simple as it could be: such a car is not affordable, and a high price means that finding the right person to pay for it could take a while.
The seller believes $150,000 is a fair price, but they also enabled the Make Offer option on eBay to allow further negotiations. You can click this button if you want the car but have another deal in mind, and you can start from here if you’re interested in this Corvette.
Photo: eBay seller capefear96terry I can’t stress enough how important it is to see the car in person before making an offer because not everything you see online also matches real life. A walkaround video would also come in handy, and photos taken during the restoration should help a potential buyer figure out if this Corvette received the top refresh advertised on eBay.
If you want to see it with your eyes, you’ll need to pack your bags for a trip all the way to Delray Beach, Florida. The listing will expire in 19 days, so you have enough time to convince your significant other that you need another classic Corvette and arrange an in-person inspection with the seller.
